p: Looking for a better way to host and ticket your events? Here are the top Eventbrite alternatives - and why Partiful might be the one you've been waiting for.
Eventbrite has been around long enough that it's basically become a verb. But that doesn't mean it's the right tool for every event, or every host.

Whether you're frustrated by high fees, a clunky guest experience, or a platform that feels more like a marketplace than a community, you're not alone. A growing number of hosts are looking for Eventbrite alternatives that better fit the way they actually throw events.
Here's what's missing from Eventbrite, and why Partiful is the alternative worth switching to.
Eventbrite works. But it comes with real trade-offs that add up quickly:

Non-curated discovery. Your event gets listed in a crowded marketplace alongside thousands of others. There's no social context, no curation, and no built-in reason for someone to choose your event over the next one.
No social layer. Guests buy a ticket and get a confirmation email. That's it. There's no way for attendees to see who else is going, no social buzz, and no organic sharing built into the experience.
Email-only communication, with limited SMS. Reaching your guests means sending emails that often go unread. Reliable SMS blasts to all attendees are paywalled or unavailable.
Co-hosting is paywalled. Adding a co-host or admin to help manage your event costs extra. For anyone running events with a team, that's a frustrating limitation.
No customization. Every Eventbrite page looks like every other Eventbrite page. Your brand, your vibe, and your community identity don't come through.
The best ticketing platforms do more than process payments. Here's what actually matters:
Organic discovery. Does the platform help your event reach new people through real social connections, not just a generic search feed?
A social event page. Can guests see who else is attending? Social proof is one of the most powerful drivers of ticket sales.
Direct guest communication. Can you reach attendees via SMS - not just email - with updates and reminders?
Free co-hosting and admin tools. Running events with a team shouldn't cost extra.
Customizable, beautiful event pages. Your event page should reflect your brand, not look like a generic checkout form.

Partiful is the ticketing platform guests actually want to use. Millions of people already plan their social lives on Partiful - from birthdays and dinners to house parties and community events. With Partiful Ticketing, that same social energy now powers paid events too.
Here's how Partiful stacks up on the things that matter:

Large organic discovery. Partiful has a local event feed called Explore, where millions of monthly visitors go to discover events. Your ticketed event shows up alongside the best things happening in your city. /blog/post/how-to-host-a-comedy-night.description: Everything you need to host a comedy night - from finding a venue and booking comedians to structuring your lineup, selling tickets, and running a tight show.
h1: How to Host a Comedy Night
h2: Set the room up for success
p: From booking comedians to selling tickets and running the room, here's everything you need to pull off a great comedy night.
A great comedy night is one of the most fun events you can throw - for the audience, the performers, and you. It also takes more planning than it looks like from the audience's perspective.
Whether you're hosting a one-off show, a recurring open mic, or a headline event, here's how to do it right.
Comedy is about intimacy. The best comedy rooms are small enough that the comedian feels close to the audience - not performing at them across a cavernous space.
What to look for in a comedy venue:
A defined performance area. Even a small raised platform focuses attention and signals to the audience that something is happening.
Good acoustics. A room with hard floors and bare walls creates echo. Soft furnishings, curtains, and carpet absorb sound and make voices cleaner.
Controlled lighting. You want to be able to dim the house lights and spotlight the performer.
A quiet back-of-house. Kitchen noise, street noise, and bar clatter are comedy killers.
Appropriate capacity. A room of 50 people that's full feels electric. A room of 200 that's half-empty feels like a failure - even if the crowd is great.
Bars with back rooms, art spaces, restaurants with private dining rooms, and even large living rooms all work well for smaller shows.
How you find and book talent depends on the scale of your show:
For open mics: Post a sign-up form and spread the word in local comedy communities. Most cities have active Facebook groups, subreddits, or Discord servers for comedians looking for stage time.
For curated lineups: Attend open mics and local shows, take note of who gets consistent laughs, and reach out directly. Most emerging comedians are reachable on Instagram.
For headline shows: Contact comedians through their booking email (usually in their Instagram or website bio) or through a manager or booking agent for more established names.
Be clear upfront about: the date and time, expected audience size, set length, and whether you're paying (and how much). Respect comedians' time - they have a craft and a business.
A well-run comedy show has a clear structure. A typical format for a 90-minute show:

MC / Host – Opens the show, warms up the crowd, introduces each act, and closes the night. This is one of the hardest jobs in the room. Find someone who can handle crowd energy and fill unexpected gaps.
Opening acts (2–3 comedians, 5–10 min each) – Sets the tone, builds energy, keeps the bar moving.
Feature act (15–20 min) – A stronger, more established comic who bridges the opener and headliner.
Intermission (optional, 10–15 min) – Lets guests refresh drinks and the room reset before the headliner.
Headliner (20–30 min) – The main draw. Close on a high note.
Comedy lives and dies by the room dynamic. A few things that make a real difference:
Seat people close together. Laughter is contagious. Sparse seating kills it.
Dim the lights before the show starts. This signals that something is beginning and gets people's attention off their phones.
Start on time. Late starts kill momentum and frustrate performers and audience alike.
Manage the bar. Drink service during the show should be minimal and quiet. Loud drink orders mid-set are disruptive.
Have a phone policy. Even a gentle request - "phones away or on silent during sets" - goes a long way.

Advance tickets are one of the most important things you can do for a comedy night. They give you a real headcount, reduce no-shows, and make the night feel like an actual event rather than a casual hang.

After the show, post highlights and tag the comedians. A well-documented show becomes content that promotes your next one. If it went well, lock in the next date while the energy is high - recurring shows build loyal audiences faster than one-offs.

h1: How to Run a Pop-Up Market
p: A practical guide to organizing a pop-up market - from finding vendors and securing a space to promoting the event and making sure it actually runs smoothly.

Pop-up markets are having a moment. Independent makers, food vendors, vintage sellers, and small brands are all looking for the same thing: a well-organized, well-attended market where they can sell to real people and build their following.
If you want to be the person who organizes that market, this guide is for you.
The most successful pop-up markets have a clear identity. Before you do anything else, get specific about what your market is for:

What kind of vendors will you feature? Handmade goods, vintage clothing, local food and drink, plants, art, candles, ceramics? A focused theme attracts more targeted vendors and a more engaged audience than a generic market.
What's the vibe? Weekend morning farmers' market energy? Evening social market with a DJ and cocktails? Holiday gift fair? The atmosphere shapes every other decision.
Who is your audience? Knowing who you're building this for helps you choose the right location, the right vendors, and the right promotional channels.
A clear identity also makes the market easier to promote - people share things they can describe easily.
The venue makes or breaks a pop-up market. You need space for vendor tables, foot traffic flow, and ideally some shelter if you're outdoors.
Outdoor spaces: Parking lots, parks, courtyards, and rooftops. Great for daytime markets. Make sure you have a rain plan or contingency date.
Indoor venues: Warehouses, event spaces, galleries, and large retail stores. More controlled environment, easier to manage flow.
Partner venues: Breweries, coffee shops, and restaurants often welcome pop-up markets because they drive foot traffic and bar/drink sales. This can reduce or eliminate venue rental costs.
When evaluating a space, think about: capacity, power access (for vendors who need it), restroom access, parking or transit access, and any permits required.
Vendors are what make a market worth attending. Start recruiting early - good vendors book out quickly, especially for weekend dates.
Post a vendor application on Instagram and in local maker and small business community groups
Reach out directly to makers and brands you already love and think fit the vibe
Tap your existing network - friends with side businesses, people you've bought from at other markets
What to include in your vendor application:
Table size and what's included (table, chairs, power, etc.)
What categories of vendors you're looking for
Expectations around setup, breakdown, and cross-promotion
Be selective. A curated market with 20 great vendors outperforms a sprawling market with 60 mediocre ones every time.
Running a pop-up market involves more operational complexity than most first-time organizers expect. Here's what to sort out in advance:
Permits. Check local requirements for temporary markets. You may need a special event permit, a temporary food handler's license (for food vendors), or both.
Vendor layout. Create a floor plan before the day. Think about traffic flow - the best spots are near the entrance and along natural foot traffic paths.
Setup and breakdown windows. Give vendors clear arrival times, and build in buffer before doors open for setup issues.
Power and Wi-Fi. Know which vendors need power for card readers or lighting and make sure you can accommodate them.
Signage. Clear directional signs improve the experience for guests and make the market feel professional.
Some pop-up markets are free entry - and that's a valid choice for maximizing foot traffic. But there are real benefits to selling even a low-cost ticket:
You get an accurate headcount for capacity planning
Paid attendees are more likely to actually show up
Ticket revenue can offset venue and production costs
It signals that the market is a curated, quality event

p: The complete playbook for getting people genuinely excited about your event - before, during, and after.
You can have the best event in the world and still have empty seats if nobody knows about it. Social media is your most powerful (and cheapest) promotional tool - but only if you use it right.
Here's a practical, no-fluff guide to promoting your event on social media, whether you're running a house party, a live show, a pop-up, or a community gathering.

Most people announce their event too late. Give yourself at least two to three weeks of promotional runway. The earlier you share, the more time people have to plan around it - and the more opportunity you have to build momentum.
2–3 weeks out: Announce the event. Share the link. Create the initial buzz.
1 week out: Post a reminder. Share a behind-the-scenes preview or detail that makes it feel more real.
2–3 days out: Post urgency content - capacity limits, ticket availability, final details.
Day of: Post a "doors open" story or countdown. Tag the venue if applicable.
You don't need to be everywhere. Focus on where your audience actually is.
Instagram – Best for visual events. Use Stories with a link sticker, Reels for behind-the-scenes content, and feed posts for the official announcement.
TikTok – Great for events with a strong visual or entertainment angle. Authentic, low-production content tends to perform better than polished ads.
Twitter / X – Useful for community events in niche spaces (tech, comedy, art). The text-first format is good for announcements and engaging with your audience directly.
Facebook – Still effective for certain demographics and community groups. Events posted in local Facebook groups can drive significant reach.
Group chats – Don't underestimate WhatsApp, iMessage, or Telegram. Sharing your Partiful link in the right group chats can be more effective than any post.
The best event promotion doesn't feel like promotion. It feels like content people actually want to see and share.
The reveal. Announce the event with a well-designed graphic or a short video that captures the vibe. Your Partiful event page can serve as the landing page.
Behind the scenes. Show the planning process - scouting the venue, designing the flyer, setting up the space. People love to feel like insiders.
Social proof. Share that tickets are selling, spots are filling, or notable people are coming. Seeing others commit reduces hesitation.
Countdowns. Instagram's countdown sticker in Stories creates real urgency and lets followers set a reminder.
Guest reposts. When attendees share your event or tag you, repost it. This multiplies reach and validates the event for people on the fence.
Every post should link back to a single destination - your event page. This is where the RSVP or ticket purchase happens, and it's what converts interest into attendance.

A Partiful event page is built for this. It's visually customizable, shows who's attending (which creates its own social pull), and lets you send SMS updates to everyone who's RSVP'd. When the event page itself is shareable and social, promotion gets easier - your guests do some of it for you.
The most credible promotion comes from people who are actually going. Make it easy for them to spread the word:

Create a shareable graphic they can repost

After the event, post a recap. Thank your attendees. Tag people. Share highlights. This content becomes the foundation for promoting your next one.

The best social media promotion is an extension of a genuinely good event. If people had a great time, they'll post about it, share it, and come back next time. Focus on making the event worth talking about - then give people the tools to talk about it.

h1: How to Run a Paid Workshop (and Sell Out Every Seat)
h2: Start with a workshop people can explain in one sentence
Price the seat around materials, time, and the room
Cap the room before you sell tickets
Make the invite do the selling
Turn one workshop into a series
Why Partiful works well for paid workshops
p: A practical guide to pricing, ticketing, filling the room, and turning one workshop into a recurring series.

Pottery, candle-making, cooking, sip-and-paint, floral design, film photography, journaling — workshops are how people learn a craft and meet others doing the same thing. They’re also one of the most natural events to charge for: people expect to pay for materials, instruction, and an experience. The hard part was never the teaching. It was pricing it, selling the seats, getting people through the door, and not drowning in Venmo requests. Here’s how to run a paid workshop end to end — and the easiest way to set the whole thing up.

A sellable workshop has a clear promise: guests should know what they’ll learn, what they’ll make, and why it feels worth leaving the house for. “Ceramics night” is vague. “Make a hand-built mug you can actually use” is concrete. “Beginner floral arranging” is fine. “Build a farmers market bouquet and take it home” is better.

Before you publish, write the pitch like you’re texting a friend: what it is, who it’s for, what’s included, and what they’ll leave with. That short description becomes the spine of your invite, your social copy, and your reminder messages.

Start with your real costs: materials per person, venue or table fee, instructor time, assistant help, snacks, payment processing, and a small buffer for no-shows or broken supplies. Then add your margin. If the workshop is intimate, hands-on, or includes take-home materials, don’t race to the cheapest price — people are paying for guidance and a finished experience, not just supplies.

A simple formula: materials + space + labor + buffer + profit, divided by your target number of seats. If the number feels high, improve the perceived value before lowering the price: better photos, a clearer outcome, a more intimate cap, or a small add-on like a take-home guide.

The best workshop size is the number of people you can meaningfully help. For hands-on classes, that usually means fewer seats than the room technically fits. A tight cap makes the event feel more special, keeps the instructor from running around all night, and gives guests a better reason to buy early.

If you’re testing a new format, start smaller. Ten people who have a great time are more valuable than thirty people who feel ignored. Once the flow is smooth, you can add another date, not just more chairs.

Your event page should answer every question someone needs before buying: date, time, location, price, what’s included, experience level, refund policy, what to bring, and whether guests can come alone. Use a photo that shows the vibe, not just the finished object. People want to picture themselves there.

Partiful makes this easier because the invite can hold the whole experience: the design, the ticket, the guest list, reminders, and updates. Guests don’t need to DM you for the Venmo, and you don’t need a spreadsheet to know who paid.

A workshop rarely sells out from one post. Launch to your warmest audience first: past guests, friends, regulars, collaborators, and people who have already shown interest. Then post publicly with the strongest hook and a clear call to buy a seat. Follow up with scarcity when it’s real: “six seats left,” “last day for early bird,” or “adding a second date if this fills.”

The best promo content shows proof: materials arriving, the setup, a previous guest’s finished piece, the menu, the table, or a short video of the process. Make it feel like an event people can already imagine joining.

Get more traction on your event by setting it to "public". Events marked "Public" on Partiful get suggested to friends-of-guests and are more likely to be featured on Partiful's Explore page, a curated catalogue of the best events in each city.

A good reminder is not just “see you tomorrow.” Tell guests when to arrive, what to bring, where to park, whether food or drinks are included, and how long the session will run. If the workshop involves drying, firing, pickup, or digital files, say exactly what happens after the event.
With Partiful, you can message the guest list in one place, so last-minute updates don’t get buried across DMs, email threads, and payment notes.

h1: How to Start a Supper Club (and Sell Out Every Seat)
h2: Start with a point of view
Choose the format before the menu
Price tickets from the bottom up
Make the invite feel like the dinner
Sell the first seats to your warmest circle

Turn one dinner into a community
Why Partiful works well for supper clubs
p: A practical guide to planning the menu, pricing seats, selling tickets, and turning one dinner into a community.

Supper clubs are having a moment — intimate, ticketed dinners where strangers become regulars and the table is the whole point. They’re also one of the easiest events to start: you don’t need a restaurant, a liquor license, or a marketing budget. You need a menu, a room, a price, and a way to sell the seats. Here’s how to do all of it, step by step.

A supper club works best when it feels like more than “dinner.” Give it a reason to exist: seasonal produce, regional comfort food, a cookbook you love, a singles table, a natural wine night, a neighborhood potluck with tickets, or a chef’s menu served in your apartment. The point of view makes the event easier to name, easier to describe, and easier for guests to share.

If you’re starting from scratch, keep the first concept narrow. “A 14-seat pasta dinner with orange wine and tiramisu” is more compelling than “a food event.” People buy tickets faster when they can picture the table.

Decide whether your supper club is seated, family-style, grazing, or a hybrid. A seated multi-course dinner feels polished but takes more timing. Family-style is warmer and easier to serve. A casual standing format can work for snacks, drinks, and mingling, but it should still have a clear food moment so guests feel like the ticket was worth it.

For a first event, three to four courses is plenty: a snack or welcome bite, a main dish, a side or salad, and dessert. Build a menu you can execute without disappearing into the kitchen for the whole night.

The room sets the ceiling, but the kitchen sets the real limit. Think about how many plates you can serve hot, how much prep space you have, how many people can sit comfortably, and whether guests need room to move around. A smaller table that feels intentional beats a packed room that feels improvised.
Start with 10 to 16 seats if you’re hosting at home. That is usually enough energy to feel social, but small enough to manage the food, pacing, and conversation without a full staff.

Add up the actual costs first: groceries, drinks, flowers, candles, plates or rentals, payment processing, cleanup help, and your own time. Then decide what margin makes the work worthwhile. If you’re charging for seats, the ticket should cover more than ingredients — it should reflect planning, hosting, cooking, and the experience you’re creating.

A simple formula: total costs + host fee + buffer, divided by the number of seats. If the price feels too low, you may be underpaying yourself. If it feels too high, improve the value with clearer storytelling, better photos, a smaller guest cap, or a more memorable menu.

Your event page is the first course. Use a name, image, and description that make the table feel real. Include the date, time, neighborhood or venue, price, menu notes, dietary accommodations, refund policy, and whether guests can come solo. The more confident the page feels, the less you’ll need to answer the same questions in DMs.
Partiful is especially useful here because the invite can be designed like a social event, while still handling tickets, RSVPs, guest messaging, and capacity in one place.

The first few tickets create momentum. Share the event privately with friends, past guests, coworkers, regulars, or people who have asked about your food before. Once there are real names on the guest list, the public post feels less like an announcement and more like something already happening.

When you post publicly, lead with the experience, not the logistics. Show the table, the menu draft, the ingredients, the playlist, or a previous dinner moment. Then make the call to action direct: buy a seat, join the waitlist, or send it to the friend you’d bring.
Learn more about selling tickets on Partiful.

Food matters, but pacing matters just as much. Decide what guests do when they arrive, when drinks are poured, when everyone sits, when each course lands, and how the night ends. A short welcome, a printed menu, or a quick toast can make the dinner feel considered without making it formal.

If guests don’t all know each other, seed the room intentionally. Put natural connectors near quieter guests, avoid seating only friend groups together, and give people an easy first conversation topic — the menu, the neighborhood, or how they found the dinner.

A day or two before the dinner, remind guests of the arrival time, address, transportation notes, menu expectations, and anything they should bring. If the location is private, you can share the exact address closer to the event. If there are dietary notes, confirm them before you shop.
Good reminders reduce no-shows and make the event feel organized. They also free you from answering scattered texts while you’re trying to prep.

The follow-up is where a supper club becomes a supper club, not just a one-off dinner. Send photos, thank guests, ask what they’d want next, and give attendees first access to the next table. If someone couldn’t get a seat, invite them to the waitlist before posting publicly again.
Over time, regulars become the core of the room. They bring friends, introduce people, and help the dinner feel alive before the first course lands.
Create an Org Profile on Partiful that guests can Follow to keep up with your events.

Supper clubs are social by nature, so the ticketing should feel social too. Partiful lets you create an invite people actually want to open, sell seats directly, cap attendance, message guests, collect RSVPs, and keep the guest list visible in a way that builds excitement.

Instead of sending one payment link, one form, one reminder thread, and one address text, you can run the whole dinner from the event page. Guests know where to go, what they paid for, who’s coming, and what to expect.

h1: Can You Sell Tickets on Facebook? What Actually Works in 2026
h2: What Facebook Events can and can't do
What Facebook is still useful for
p: Facebook Events have changed a lot. Here's what still works for selling tickets in 2026 — and what to use instead.

Facebook Events have been around long enough that plenty of hosts still rely on them as their main event tool. But if you're trying to sell tickets and run a properly managed event, Facebook has real limitations that add up quickly.
Facebook lets you create an event page, invite people, and post updates. Some setups let you link out to a ticketing platform. But as a full ticketing solution, it falls short:
No reliable native ticketing - Facebook's built-in ticketing features are limited and inconsistently available. Most hosts end up linking to a third-party platform anyway.
No real guest list management - "Going" on a Facebook Event doesn't mean much. There's no payment confirmation, no QR code, and no way to know who's actually coming until they show up.
Limited guest communication - updates posted to a Facebook Event page don't guarantee your guests will see them. The algorithm controls what surfaces in their feeds.
Declining relevance for younger audiences - if your crowd skews under 35, Facebook Events may not be where they're looking.
That said, it's not useless - especially for specific audiences:
Local community groups - posting in a relevant local Facebook group can still drive meaningful reach for neighborhood events, markets, and community gatherings
Older demographics - if your audience skews 35 and up, Facebook Events remain a relevant discovery channel
Paid ads - Meta's ad platform can be effective for reaching targeted audiences around your event if you have a promotion budget

Use Facebook for reach and a dedicated ticketing platform for everything else. Create your event on Partiful, get your link, and share it in your Facebook Event, your community groups, and anywhere else your audience is.

Partiful handles the ticket sale, the guest list, check-in, and communication - so you're not cobbling together a functional event management system from Facebook's limited toolset. And unlike a Facebook Event, a Partiful event page shows guests who else is attending - which creates social proof and drives more ticket sales through genuine word of mouth.

h1: Can You Sell Tickets on Instagram? Here's How It Works
h2: What Instagram is genuinely good for
How to drive Instagram traffic to your ticket page
Why Partiful pairs well with Instagram
p: There's no native ticket checkout on Instagram - but here's exactly how to use your bio, Stories, and DMs to drive real ticket sales.

Instagram is where most events get discovered. It's great for building hype, posting flyers, and reaching new audiences. But when it comes to actually selling tickets, the answer is more nuanced than most hosts expect.

You can't sell tickets natively on Instagram. There's no built-in checkout for events, no ticket delivery system, no guest list, and no QR code check-in. What Instagram does - and does very well - is drive traffic to wherever you are actually selling tickets.
The most effective setup: use Instagram for promotion, and a dedicated platform like Partiful for the sale itself. Here's how that works in practice:
Create your ticketed event on Partiful and get your event link
Add the link to your Instagram bio or use the link sticker in Stories
Post your flyer, a short video, or a behind-the-scenes clip with a clear call to action: "Tickets in bio" or "Link in Stories"
Guests tap through, land on your Partiful event page, and buy in a few taps
Even though it can't sell tickets directly, Instagram is one of your most powerful promotional tools:
Stories with link stickers - a well-timed Story pointing to your event page is still one of the highest-converting promotional formats available
Reels for reach - short video content can reach people well beyond your existing followers
Feed posts for credibility - a polished announcement signals the event is real and worth showing up for
Tagging collaborators - every performer or vendor you tag shares your event with their audience for free
Put your Partiful link in your bio as soon as tickets go live
Use Instagram's countdown sticker in Stories to build anticipation
Share capacity updates - "Only 25 spots left" creates urgency that converts
Repost when guests share your event - their followers become your potential audience

When someone clicks your Instagram link and lands on a Partiful event page, they don't just see a checkout form. They see who else is going - friends, mutuals, people they recognize. That social layer does something Instagram alone can't: it turns curiosity into commitment. Seeing that people you know are already going is one of the most powerful reasons to buy a ticket.

/blog/post/the-cuntiest-chess-club-in-lo.description: A nightlife-infused chess scene and your next Thursday night move
h1: The Cuntiest Chess Club in Los Angeles
h3: Give us the origin story—how did Rookie Chess come to life?
Who actually shows up? Is it mostly beginners, or are all levels welcome?
If someone’s never played chess before but is curious, how would you encourage them to come to a meetup?
Okay, set the scene: What’s the vibe at your events?
Seems like a good place to find a new crush…
How many games run at once?
In your professional opinion, is there any correlation between skill level and swag?
What’s a chess stereotype that tends to be true?
What’s a chess stereotype that’s completely false?
Describe Rookie Chess in one word.
Why do people keep coming back?
If Rookie Chess were a single chess piece, which one would it be and why?
p: This nightlife-infused chess scene is your next Thursday night move

Rookie Chess League isn’t just another Los Angeles chess club—it’s where friendly, competitive play meets cocktails and curated chaos. Born from a dramatic club split (lore incoming 👀), RCL brings a nightlife energy to the 64 squares, drawing everyone from national masters to total beginners (and even a cat named Dante).

Every Thursday, players gather for fast-paced games, free one-on-one lessons, and outfits as sharp as their strategies. Whether you’re here to play or just soak up the scene, there’s always a seat waiting.

The origins of RCL are quite unique. As co-founders, we previously ran a well-known chess club in the area. However, after a falling out with its founder, we decided to start our own free event. Many community members joined us in the transition, and their support has meant a lot. 🫶🏽 Our longtime supporter and homegirl, Jessie, actually gave us the name “Rookie” when we asked everyone what their favorite chess piece was!

We have a great mix of newbies and advanced players every week, and all levels are welcome. We have had 5 national masters show up for a single event, which isn’t super common for most clubs. They tend to frequent as well.

We tell all new players to come and sign up for a free 1-on-1 lesson if they are totally new. It helps them learn chess and get to meet someone right away. Mateo, one of our cofounders, leads the lessons, so it’s a nice introduction to the community and the game.

It's Thursday night, you walk into our event, and you hear great music playing, people mingling, drinks flowing, and the occasional stop clock being slapped. It’s exciting, organized chaos! We like to get our weekends started early, which is why our events are always on Thursdays. And if you aren’t all that into chess, we always have amazing DJs spinning during the event, or there are other activities at each establishment that people can do if they need a chess break.

We have had a few meet their s/o at the event, but no one has tied the knot yet. We are awaiting those invites when they happen, tho 👀 We also recently had our first chess couple breakup and are patiently waiting to see who gets custody of us. We also have someone who brings their cat, Dante, almost whenever he comes.
We normally bring about 40 boards, so that's around 80 people playing at once. This seems to be the best number for a good mix of mingling and chess.

There is no real correlation between the two; HOWEVER, many of our attendees LOVE to show out at each event. Some come in chess-themed clothes, suits and ties, veils, gloves, dramatic trench coats, office siren core, heels— we’ve seen it all. We like to think our attendees dress for the occasion, and everyone looks great in what makes them feel the most confident.

Everyone who plays has an ego; it’s completely true; however, it's a playful ego. We’re all just self-righteous nerds who found each other and created a community around this super dorky game that we all take a little too seriously.

You can’t be good unless you’ve been playing your whole life! Some of the best chess players that attend have only been playing for a year or so. Anyone can learn chess at any age and still become a great chess player.
CUNT (this is literally our tagline for C U Next Thursday)

People love IRL games, and it’s a great way for people to connect. Chess encourages people to chat and helps break the ice by being a mutual interest. It’s really hard to meet like-minded people in the wild (outside in the real world), and chess allows people with a shared interest to connect.

h1: An NYC Film Club That’s So Bad It’s Good
h3: Give us the origin story — how did BFC come to life? How has it evolved over time?
How does BFC actually work? Who picks the films, and what’s the process like?
What’s the difference between “your film bro’s movie club” and BFC?
If your film club were a director, who would it be and why?

What’s one movie that’s completely off-limits for your club—and why?

What’s a film opinion you hold that would probably get you banned from other film clubs?
What’s the best theatre in NYC? Why?
What’s your favorite post-film spot to debrief and why?
p: A convo with Lily & Sofia on orchestrating a meeting of unusual minds

Bad Film Club isn’t your film bro’s movie club—it’s more of a cinematic cult for the baddies of NYC built on community, conversation, and a shared love of the big-screen. More than just another movie club, it's a self-proclaimed “judgment-free" space where popcorn lovers and film snobs can coexist in harmony.

What started as a simple New Year’s resolution between best friends Lily and Sofia has turned into a thriving film club in NYC, drawing cinephiles who want more than just another repertory screening. If you've ever dreamed of sipping a PBR while giggling through Blue Velvet, Bad Film Club is your new favorite way to experience movies in the city.

Bad Film Club started as a pipedream-turned-shared New Year’s resolution between two best friends. We weren’t trying to run a marathon or join a run club, we just wanted a community that we felt didn’t exist yet: a group of people like us who love celebrating everything that both movies and the moviegoing experience have to offer.

Bad Film Club meets in-person the last Thursday of every month. For nearly a year–one year in April!–our formula has been consistent: we pick a movie, pull up with our members (dubbed: “the baddies”), and then go to a bar to chat about it. We work together to select the movies, which are mostly repertory releases with a few exciting new movies thrown in. Lily tends to handle the logistics, including coordinating with theaters and members, while Sofia (aka our memelord) runs our finances and digital communications (hello Partiful).

We want everyone to feel at home with us in the movie theater, so we’ve made our barrier to entry as low as possible. All we ask is that you buy a ticket and keep an open mind. If you’re a cinephile who can name every Kurosawa movie in order, great: come to Bad Film Club. If you’re a cinesoftie who is here for the movie theater popcorn and vibes, also great: come to Bad Film Club.

A Neon-produced Nora Ephron movie directed by Luca Guadagnino avec la participation de Canal+. We’ve got witty repartee and the meetings of unusual minds but we’re unconventional and would crush at Cannes.

Our first-ever screening was Alex Garland’s Civil War (2024). Sorry to have to pun like this, but it caused a civil war. Lily is on record strongly disliking it; Sofia is on record liking it slightly above average.

When we started the club, we really leaned on our friends and their plus ones for numbers. As time has passed, the composition has shifted dramatically: many of our friends, having shepherded their own movie-loving friends to BFC, have gracefully bowed out, while those plus ones have stayed on. Tons of new folks have joined organically through connections on Letterboxd (hi Jason and Mike) or Instagram (hi Meg and Dief), and a few even through chance encounters in movie theaters. (Lily met one of our members, Corey, while chatting before a screening of Holy Motors at Paris Theater when they realized that in the past week, they had seen the same three movies at the same time across the same three theaters.)

Watching the Bad Film Club community evolve has been so incredibly rewarding. Every month, we hear from our members how special it is for them to have this opportunity to celebrate an art form they love with a group of people they might not have otherwise met.

Show up solo to Bad Film Club and you’ll leave with three new IRL friends and a dozen new Letterboxd followers. It’s unavoidable. But ritual-wise, Sofia and Lily always wait outside the theater before the show starts to greet all members, new and returning, and pass out tickets. Everyone gets a hug, and we try to introduce new folks to a returning member so they have someone to sit next to in the theater.
At the bar, new members’ first round is on us – plus a cheeky BFC sticker to take home.

500 Days of Summer (Lily) – I hate the “straight quirked up white boy falls for manic pixie dream girl” trope more than almost anything else and this is its platonic ideal (derogatory). Tarkovsky’s Stalker (Sofia) – was told by one too many people this movie would change my life, and they were right.. it did. It solidified my desire to start this club; I needed a safe space to talk about how infuriated this movie makes me.

BFC is the best friend in the romcom who kind of steals the show. Think Philip Seymour Hoffman in Along Came Polly or Carrie Fisher in When Harry Met Sally or Whoopi Goldberg in Waiting to Exhale or Judy Greer in 27 Dresses or Judy Greer in The Wedding Planner or Judy Greer in 13 Going on 30.
Seven Samurai is…boring. Don’t @ us. Also talking in theaters is sometimes fun if you can be normal and quiet and chill about it.
Ah, don’t make us pick favorites! But of the theaters BFC has visited:
For seeing and being seen as you take in your scenes: Roxy Cinema
For the city’s best movie theater popcorn: Paris Theater
For the campiest interior: AMC Lincoln Square
For your favorite in 35mm: Village East
For the repertory series: Film Forum / IFC

/blog/post/grad-party-ideas-for-the-chic.title: Grad Party Ideas for the Chic and Chaotic
/blog/post/grad-party-ideas-for-the-chic.description: The best pinterest ideas for the Class of 2025
h1: Grad Party Ideas for the Chic and Chaotic
p: The best pinterest ideas for the Class of 2025

You did it. The late nights, existential dread, and overpriced coffee all paid off—you’re officially hotter by one degree. Before adulthood fully sinks its teeth in, you deserve a moment (or a party) to celebrate everything you just conquered. Whether you’re feeling sentimental, a little unhinged, or fully refusing to grow up, we’ve got grad party ideas to match your vibe. Find a cohost, gather some supplies, and let’s make some memories.

You don’t need a Hollywood budget to make a photo booth moment. A little fabric and some clever hanging techniques go a long way. For a bold, metallic look, grab a backdrop frame and some mylar—clamp it up and call it glam. Feeling more whimsical? Drape a lace tablecloth over some rope with clothespins and pray the wind’s in a good mood. If you’re surrounded by trees, hang tinsel from the branches and lean into the woodland fairy vibe. For a rustic twist, stack and drill together a few stolen (borrowed?) wooden pallets—bonus points if you add oversized paper flowers or handwritten signs.

Let’s be honest: the cake says everything. Skip the generic “Congrats Grad” and go for something that actually speaks to your personality—think “One Degree Hotter,” “Grad U Ate,” or even just your baby photo in edible ink (the grandparents will eat it up, literally). The best cakes have a sense of humor and a clear point of view. It doesn’t have to be fancy—it just has to say what you want your final statement as a student to be. Think of it less as dessert, more as a mic drop.

You don’t need balloons with your face on them, custom matchboxes, or a bucket of disposable cameras—but you’ll be glad you had them. These are the little things that take your party from “cute” to “iconic.” Fatheads of yourself? Absolutely. Wine glass name tags? Classy. Edible flowers in drinks? Obviously. If you’re feeling especially unhinged, design a lighter with your face on it and hand them out like party favors.
It’s your party—pick a vibe, send the invite, and celebrate like the legend you are.

/blog/post/the-cost-of-late-stage-partyi.title: The Cost of Late Stage Partyism
h1: The Cost of Late Stage Partyism
p: Ticketed parties have dominated the scene for years, offering exclusivity, great DJs, and a built-in social atmosphere. This became especially true post-pandemic when leaving the house and having fun felt like a luxury. With nightclubs feeling outdated, growing disinterest in “section culture” and playing Bad Bitch Olympics, Gen Z turned to casual and inclusive parties at large venues.

Ticketed parties aren’t a novel concept. When I moved to New York in early 2022, I realized these events were the backbone of NYC’s nightlife for Black and brown young adults. Attending Everyday PPL, South House, or wherever DJ Mike Nasty was spinning during these party collective’s growing “iykyk” stage felt like winning a golden ticket and guaranteed a great time.

Their occasional nature in large cities like New York or LA made them appealing, but the elusiveness has worn off as they’ve become more frequent. Now, if you miss one party, another pops up in a few weeks. The market has become  oversaturated with new collectives trying to mimic the success of established ones. Not to mention everyone seemingly becoming DJs overnight. We love exploring new hobbies, but I can’t help but wonder if it’s a social media clout chase rather than genuine music lovers wanting to curate a vibe.

With rising demand comes rising costs, as ticket prices have almost doubled in the last three years. This, plus astronomical drink prices, has me questioning if it’s even how I want to spend my money. If I'm paying $50+ for a ticket and $20 per drink, financially, I’m no longer having fun. (R*cess*on indicator?)

Meeting people at parties can be fun, but with hook-up culture changing (see: declining), Gen Z is searching for more meaningful relationships. You meet someone on a drunken night and exchange socials in passing, but likely have low intentions of taking them seriously because of how you met–be honest.

Not to say the love of your life isn’t on the dance floor. Maybe they are! But these settings don’t always foster something long-lasting. Even platonically, when I experience the female rite of passage of bonding with another drunk girl in the bathroom and exchanging Instagrams, she still ends up becoming another random person whose stories I passively watch but never get to know.

Sometimes, you just need a night of debauchery to dance wildly with friends, though. At that point, I’d rather just go to an actual club and embrace section culture. But where do you go if you want to have fun AND meet people?

It’s almost like we need to go back to basics. The best part of the night is often the pregame anyways, so it’s only natural that collectively we’re recreating its best aspects. This is where the rise of more intimate gatherings comes in.

House parties have always been spaces for good vibes: they’re generally low-cost and comfortable because you either know or know of the host and other attendees. From a relationship-building aspect, I’m all about vetting people romantically or platonically. It’s unsettling getting someone’s Instagram at a party and having no mutuals. Knowing the person you’re romantically interested in has ties to your social circle makes diving in feel safer. It’s also easier to establish new friendships when you already have friends in common.

These intimate settings allow actual conversation without having to yell over ear-piercing music. (There's nothing worse than a guy trying to talk to you at the bar of a loud event, and he's low-key spitting in your ear.) The liquor is free, and sometimes there's food! The only dilemma? Most of Gen Z does not have homes, and the way the economy is looking...will we ever? Naturally, we’re finding other ways to mirror this energy.

Vinyl bars and listening parties are popping up all over New York. With a more laid-back, sexy feel, these spots are also great ways to discover new and niche music. I’m personally advocating to try new bars rather than a typical party every weekend with friends.

Wine For Me is a wine party that has been gaining traction by adding a new flair to the typical party scene. Speed dating events advertised around Valentine's Day had lots of interest, but I also predict more “flirting parties” popping up closer to summer.

There will always be the desire to party, but the landscape is evolving, and party groups are pivoting. From live sets like Black House Radio, Aprtment Life, Boiler Room, and now South House Live and South House Run Club, these groups understand the changing social space and the desire to party with a purpose to build community.

Maybe it’s a symptom of getting older or the fear of monotony, but the same old format is boring and played out. I’m not even advocating for parties and clubs to disappear–there will always be a time and place for them, like visiting a new city or holidays. I just think a switch up on nightlife is imminent.

What I'm searching for is balance—dancing, questionable but fun decisions, and real connection in new and exciting settings. Because at the end of the day, people want to connect more than they want to party—and they want it cheaply. So that’s what I’m chasing, and I intend to find it.

/blog/post/flamer-hosts-700-stoners-for-.title: FLAMER HOSTS 700 STONERS FOR QUEER CHURCH ON 420
/blog/post/flamer-hosts-700-stoners-for-.description: An iconic gathereing in Prospect Park to celebrate the sacred holiday
h1: FLAMER HOSTS 700 STONERS FOR QUEER CHURCH ON 420
p: An iconic gathereing in Prospect Park to celebrate the sacred holiday

On Sunday 4/20, 700 stoners gathered in Prospect Park to celebrate the sacred holiday. As 4/20 fell on Easter Sunday this year queer cannabis brand FLAMER decided to have a little twist on their annual picnic. The theme was Queer church and everyone was asked to dress in their Sunday best. And of course the flamers turned out!

From flower studded hair and hats to gothic nuns and priests, FASHION was alive and well at the FLAMER 4/20 picnic. Whether it be lacey suit ensembles or hats made from barbie dolls, this event was more than just a stoner hangout, it was a full-blown runway of queer expression, where cannabis culture met high camp and holy slay.

Some iconic babes came through to the function like Willam, who’s known for her time on Drag Race Season 4, Qween Jean, a beloved activist and costume designer, Von, a queer music artist who specializes in freaking people out, and Vas, a model + content creator known in BK for their performances as Miss Daddi.

This picnic had everything and more. Picnic blankets scattered around the peninsula by the water at Prospect park. With activities everywhere you turned. For those who love to toke and make art, there was a crafting station complete with all the materials to decorate lighters and Select vapes + pens, make angel halos, collage, and more.

People were invited to join in a wellness silent disco by tapping into the picnic’s curated playlist, sound baths by Pammy, and a guided meditation by Solonje Burnett AKA Weed Auntie. SASS provided some delicious FLAMER-420-exclusive infused chocolate truffles for people to intentionally consume before the meditation. Between the warm sun, soft grass, and sweet treats – these mindful moments were much needed and truly unforgettable.

A nun walked around passing out red joinks to the people like little weed fairies. While the sun was beating down and people passed joinks around, we also had a hydration fairy bringing people shots of coconut water w/ CBD, by Brelixi. Fun fact: CBD can help balance you out if you’re feeling a little too high. While it doesn't lessen the effects of THC, it can provide a calming moment for your body. So FLAMER loves to have CBD specialists on deck. There also were some delicious bevs from Dirty Virgin that are non-alcoholic twists on some cocktail classics like the margarita.

To lean into the post-easter-sunday-picnic-of-it-all, there were some iconic field day games like sack races and egg + spoon relays. Imagine stoned queers dressed to the nines bouncing to the finish line in child-sized sacks—it was iconic. Pure inner child joy.

FLAMER also partnered with Black and Pink NYC on an educational card-making section where guests could make cards for incarcerated queer folx. From birthdays to special holidays, these folx need all the joy they can get, so FLAMER shared the love.

In true FLAMER fashion, the 4/20 picnic was more than just a celebration—it was a joyful, queer sanctuary where community, creativity, and cannabis came together in vibrant harmony. With fashion-forward flair, mindful moments, and playful nostalgia woven throughout the day, it was a beautiful reminder that queer joy is sacred, and gathering together in radical celebration can be both healing and electric. Whether you came for the truffles, the tunes, the tokes, or just to bask in chosen family vibes, this year’s 4/20 was a high holiday to remember.

/blog/post/euro-summer-in-nyc-no-passpor.title: Euro Summer in NYC – No Passport Needed
/blog/post/euro-summer-in-nyc-no-passpor.description: The ultimate guide to channeling Amalfi, Berlin, and Ibiza—without leaving the five boroughs
h1: Euro Summer in NYC – No Passport Needed
h2: Euro Summer isn’t a location – it’s a state of mind
p: The ultimate guide to channeling Amalfi, Berlin, and Ibiza without leaving the five boroughs

Let’s be real: you’re about to scroll past Amalfi sunsets, Ibiza raves, and boat days in Dubrovnik. But some of us are staying put. And honestly? Thank God. Because New York’s Euro summer energy is unhinged, unfiltered, and right around the corner.
Take it from me, a German expat’s best friend, who’s done the rounds – Barcelona, Ibiza, Amalfi, Berlin, Lisbon, Marbella – and made it her mission to recreate the vibe right here in NYC.

Whether you’re hoping to fall in love with a European man while Baianá blares overhead, or just want to drink outside in beautiful clothes – this is your guide to doing Euro summer, without leaving the city.
Left & Middle Aperol Spritz at Bar Pisellino; Right: Aperol Spritz by the Trevi fountain in Rome
For an aperol spritz with a side of Italian flirt

This is where you go when you want espresso by day and several Aperol Spritzes by night, preferably while making intense eye contact with someone wearing Tod’s loafers. Bar Pisellino is a Roman holiday fantasy – but instead of the Trevi Fountain, it’s a West Village corner with perfect lighting, mini sandwiches, and beautiful European people at almost every table.
Pro Tip: Get there before 5:45 on weeknights to beat the line.
All enjoying the day in the new French Printemps store in the Financial District
For sipping champagne under hand-painted ceilings

This is where you go when you want to pretend you're shopping off the Champs-Élysées – even if you’re just wandering through the fragrance floor with a flute of something cold and expensive. Printemps is a Parisian daydream dropped into the Financial District, all curated fashion, dramatic florals, and hand-painted ceilings. Come for the couture, stay for the cocktails, and if you happen to lose track of time between handbags and hors d’oeuvres and ultimately pay for a facial on your way out, well, that’s kind of the point.
Pro Tip: Start with champagne at the 2nd floor bar, then wander. Every floor feels like a soft launch into a new floor of the Musée d'Orsay.
Left: A Café Select adventure; Middle & right: Me and my schnitzel at Borchardt
For schnitzel, spritzes, and the pregame that turns into the night

If you’re craving Borchardt vibes without the Berlin flight, head to Café Select. It’s not as buttoned-up, but the energy hits the same – long tables, loud friends, and drinks that keep coming. Come for the schnitzel, stay for the second round, and don’t be surprised if the whole table ends up at La Esquina after midnight.
Pro Tip: Bring a group and order the carajillo for a caffeine boost.
*My European friends inside Felix for a German futbol game*
For sports Sundays with a side of espresso martinis

Felix is where you go when you want to watch the game without giving up good outfits or better drinks. It’s loud, packed, and somehow still feels like your favorite corner of SoHo. Think jerseys mixed with Jacquemus, Aperol spritzes at noon, and bartenders who keep the energy high even when your team loses.
Pro Tip: Get there early for a table outside – it’s where the real game’s happening anyway.
Left: Beer at The Standard Biergarten; Middle & Right: Beer and bratwurst at a biergarten in Berlin
Berlin beer culture, but make it Meatpacking

This is for the girls who want to pretend they’re in Berlin – but like Berlin as imagined by someone who’s only seen the Dior Homme campaign. You’re here for the ping pong, the pretzels, and the possibility of making out with a finance bro who DJs on the side.
Pro Tip: Go on game days to watch your favorite team from the big screens. This is a scaled back Houston Hall minus the interns.
Left & Middle: night out at Gospel; similar to right: Calvin Harris rave in Ibiza
Ibiza meets warehouse rave meets accidental spiritual awakening

Dark lighting, endless dancing, and the kind of DJ set that makes you feel like you’ve ascended. Gospel is where you end up when the night spirals in the best possible way. It’s giving Ibiza with a splash of NoLita, and if you’re lucky, you’ll leave with a phone number and a new favorite house song.
Pro Tip: Have a friend with a table and wear something breathable. You will sweat.
*Left: food at Cipriani; Right: Socialista Lounge upstairs*
For Bellinis, pasta, and disappearing to the speakeasy upstairs

Come for the crisp tablecloths, stay for the after-dark shift. Cipriani is old-school Italian glamour with a side of scene – you’ll spot Rolexes, rosé, and whispered deals over lobster tagliolini. And once the espresso hits? You’re probably heading upstairs to Socialista, where the lighting’s low and everyone somehow knows each other.
Pro Tip: Order a Bellini with dinner, then “accidentally” follow the beautiful people up the stairs.
*Left: Jeans in Noho; Right: Club in Berlin*
For 2 a.m. smoke breaks and fashion week flashbacks

Jeans isn’t just a nightclub… it’s a mood, a hallway, a basement, and somehow a runway. Hidden in Noho and barely marked, it’s where the cool crowd sweats out their secrets to deep house in Margiela boots. It’s loud, it’s dark, and you’ll probably see someone you ghosted.
Pro Tip: The boy-to-girl ratio here matters. The best way in is by dressing for the part, not asking.

And in New York, that means bouncing from an Italian café to a German beer garden to a techno-fueled dance floor, all before your phone dies and you’re running around the streets of New York with a random group of friends from Amsterdam you’ll never see again.
Start your summer strong with a cheeky little spritz invite.

/blog/post/kit-volta-wants-an-gay-evil-b.title: Kit Volta Wants a "Gay Evil Boyfriend"
/blog/post/kit-volta-wants-an-gay-evil-b.description: How a dating flyer for a Gay Evil Boyfriend Became a downtown art happening
h1: Kit Volta Wants a "Gay Evil Boyfriend"
h2: The Premise: Find Me a Gay Evil Boyfriend (Please)
The Event: Speed Dating Meets Performance Art
The Aftermath: Dates, DMs, and Digital Footprints
The Takeaway: Dating Is Performance Art
p: How a dating flyer for a gay evil boyfriend became a downtown art happening

In a city oversaturated with parties, performances, and profile pics, it takes something uniquely unhinged to cut through the noise. Enter Gay Evil Boyfriend—a chaotic, genre-bending dating campaign from Kit Volta that blended physical flyers, internet culture, and live theatrical chaos into a deeply earnest attempt to fall in love (or at least go on a few dates).

Inspired in part by the surreal joy of watching Cheeseball Man devour an entire jar of cheese balls in Washington Square Park, Kit decided to take whimsy into her own hands. The experience felt oddly transcendent—“I have never felt more alive on a Saturday than that day”—and sparked her desire to create a public spectacle of her own.
Kit, an interdisciplinary interactive media artist, created the Gay Evil Boyfriend campaign as a way to get over a crush - it’s called healing, look it up.
She defines the “Gay Evil Boyfriend” as a metrosexual-coded archetype—think a straight man who paints his nails, has great photos, and listens to Clairo.

To promote the event, Kit plastered flyers outside of Ray’s Bar, Kiki’s, Dimes Square, next to the 2nd Street on Howard, along both Bedford and Jefferson Avenues, and outside of Carousel in Bushwick — places her target audience typically frequents. Each flyer had a scannable QR code that brought them to the application form. Brave strangers were able to submit themselves (or others) for the role of Gay Evil Boyfriend.

But the campaign didn’t just live in the streets. Kit revamped her Hinge profile to market the event, spent $50 on Twitter ads, and built a website that displayed randomized submissions. The chaos worked: collecting around 100 responses, including one from none other than Julian Casablancas of The Strokes (who, in true chaotic-neutral fashion, now views Kit’s stories religiously but doesn’t follow her back).
Then came the climax: a live event hosted at Telos House in East Williamsburg.

Ninety people RSVP’d via Partiful and Kit’s friends dressed as office sirens to help to present submission data while AI-generated visuals looped in the background like a fever dream. There was a live speed dating round between Kit and five applicants (four men, one woman). At the end, the sirens crowned the “Most Gay,” “Most Evil,” and, of course, “Most Boyfriend.”

Kit has gone on several dates with people she met through the project. What Is New York reposted the flyers. What Is New York Dating covered the campaign. It’s safe to say a niche but mighty cultural moment was born.

But beyond the Instagram reposts and potential romances, Gay Evil Boyfriend offered something rarer: a new framework for what dating can look like when it’s infused with humor, vulnerability, and an unapologetic sense of camp.

For Kit, the project wasn’t just about dating—it was a test of what happens when you design intimacy like an art piece. It was her first experiment involving live performance, user-generated content, and real-time participation. And New York ate it up.

Kit’s biggest learning? People want this. New Yorkers are desperate for dating events that aren’t dead-eyed speed dating nights at Murray Hill bars. They want weird. They want narrative. They want a little evil.
Also: if you’re trying to get over a crush, launching a viral queer dating experiment might just be the way to do it.

/blog/post/i-only-threw-this-party-for-y.title: I Only Threw This Party For You: The Most Iconic Summer Parties on Film
/blog/post/i-only-threw-this-party-for-y.description: Romance, existential hangovers, and the last days of our youth
h1: I Only Threw This Party For You: The Most Iconic Summer Parties on Film
h2: The Romantic Blur: The Party as a Portal Into (or out of) Love
The Existential Hangover: When the Party Isn’t a Release, But a Reckoning
The Last Days of Youth: Summer Parties as Rites of Passage
p: Romance, existential hangovers, and the last days of our youth

There’s something so irresistible about a party scene in a film. Maybe it’s the perfect lighting, the just-loud enough music, the beautifully choreographed movements, or a feeling that anything can happen in the next five-minutes: a confession, a kiss, a fight, or a breakdown. Especially in summer films, parties set in sizzling heat carry a different kind of cinematic electricity. Beyond soundtracks or aesthetics, the best summer party films confront some deeper emotional truth, or the universal feelings that simmer just below the surface. They mark turning points, mask deeper tensions, or capture fleeting moments of freedom and desire. Onscreen, the party isn’t just a backdrop, but a crucible. Characters can choose to either shed their inhibitions or cling to performance. The night might end in euphoria or completely unravel, but either way, the party changes something or someone. As viewers, we’re drawn into the mess, the magic, and the meaning in all the shiny glitter.
This article is a love letter to those scenes: the iconic summer parties featured on film that make us wish we were there, or maybe grateful that we weren’t.
Love doesn’t usually arrive with a formal invitation. It finds its way in through the music, the sneaky glances across the room, and the late-night conversations that feel like confessions.

In Call Me by Your Name, the scenic summer haze is pierced by a party scene that captures the ache of wanting someone you can’t quite have. Set in Northern Italy... A life-changing summer romance forever changes Elio when he meets Oliver. In this scene, Elio watches Oliver dance with another woman. As we linger on Elio’s face, we feel everything: yearning, jealousy, desire. Elio joins in on the dance floor: to just let loose or maybe to get ever so closer to Oliver. The party is background noise to a powerful longing and heartbreak unfolding onscreen.

Someone Great is a bittersweet romantic dramedy about Jenny, a music journalist, reeling from a break-up with her long-term boyfriend right before she’s set to move across the country for her dream job. Her two best friends help her have one last epic night out by finding last minute tickets for her favorite summer concert series, revisiting old haunts, crashing parties, and reckoning with a version of herself that she’s leaving behind in New York City. It’s a love story about friendship, change, and letting go, with a killer soundtrack and a big emotional heart. We weave in and out of their love story throughout the film, but when she finally bumps into her ex at the party, Jenny learns to finally let go. The lights are low, but suddenly everything is clear.
These party scenes mark moments when love becomes unavoidable or impossibly out of reach.
Some parties feel less like a celebration and more like an identity crisis in real time. While the drinks are flowing and the music’s loud, underneath it: something’s slowly unraveling.

In The Worst Person in the World, Julie stumbles into a stranger’s wedding on her way home and decides to infiltrate it. She's in a long-term relationship with someone else at this point, but there's a creeping restlessness in her life. Everything feels like it's closing in: expectations, timelines, definitions of who she should be. And then she meets Eivind at the party. The scene isn’t overtly romantic in the conventional sense but the chemistry is immediate, palpable, and rebellious. They make a game of seeing how close they can get to cheating without technically crossing a line: sharing secrets, confessing petty crimes, brushing fingers, smelling each other’s sweat. It’s playful, but also deeply vulnerable. The thrill comes not just from the flirtation, but from the recognition. They see each other in a way no one else at that party (or in their lives) does. For Julie, nothing happens but everything changes, stumbling into a version of herself she didn’t know was possible.

In The Graduate, Ben walks through a suffocating cocktail party, surrounded by adults asking about his post-grad future (yuck). It's not a wild, debauched night. It’s quiet, formal, and deeply uncomfortable. He’s freshly graduated, directionless, and already spiraling. It’s at that stiff, claustrophobic party Ben realizes adulthood might be a trap. The party becomes a visual metaphor for the dread of entering a life that doesn’t feel like it is entirely yours. These are the parties that don’t offer catharsis, but confrontation with age, with feeling like a failure, and with yourself.
These scenes remind us that not every party offers joy or even release. Sometimes, they simply turn up the volume on everything you're trying to ignore.

Some parties feel like endings. Not in a dramatic, explosive way, but in the quiet, aching sense that a version of you is about to be left behind: your teenage self, your first love, the dreams for the future. These scenes are messy, hilarious, a little tragic, and always tinged with that unmistakable feeling that everything’s about to change.

In Booksmart, Amy and Molly, two academically driven best friends who’ve avoided the typical high school party scene, decide to make up for lost time by cramming four years of missed experiences into one unforgettable night before graduation. What begins as a mission to “go wild” spirals into a journey of emotional honesty, miscommunications, and beautifully awkward revelations.

Mamma Mia! is a completely different kind of coming-of-age: one where youth is looked at through the dual lenses of nostalgia and reinvention. On a fictional Greek island drenched in sunlight and backed by an entirely ABBA soundtrack, Sophie throws a pre-wedding bash in an effort to discover the true identity of who her father really is. The party-filled (one might even say... partiful) days leading up to her wedding transform into a reunion, a confessional, and a celebration of love in all its complex and complicated forms. Youth here is something to be re-lived, reclaimed, or let go of, preferably while singing completely wasted under the hot sun, and with the help of a few famous Swedish pop anthems.
These are the parties where you grow up and long for the past at the same time.

The best summer party scenes aren’t really about the party at all but a transformation. Under the heat, characters fall in love, fall apart, grow up, or come undone. But summer never lasts as long as we want it to. The party captures a version of us on the brink of change: restless, in motion, and distilled into something fleeting and true.
Enter the summer state of mind with a summer solstice movie night 🌞

/blog/post/invite-everyone-you-know-to-a.title: Invite Everyone You Know to a Bar
/blog/post/invite-everyone-you-know-to-a.description: My friends and I followed a bit to its insane conclusion…and we urge you to follow our lead.
h1: Invite Everyone You Know to a Bar
p: My friends and I followed a bit to its insane conclusion…and we urge you to follow our lead

It started out as a joke. My dear friend Emily asked our sacred groupchat of NYC friends what would happen if she invited every Hinge date she had to a bar at once. After volleying that hilarious yet horrifying idea around for some time, we began to ask: what if it was just…every person? What would ensue?

My group of friends can’t back away from a bit. The idea of inviting everyone we know to a bar at once charmed us too much to pass up. We found a date in September 2024 that worked for our group of 7, made a Partiful, and started sending invitations at a truly bewildering rate.

When I say inviting everyone we know, I mean it in the truest sense of the word. Year-old past situationships. People from high school we hadn’t talked to in years, but knew were floating around the city. Two-job-ago coworkers. Camp friends of yore. Cousins and their respective fiancés. When we commit, we commit hard.

Predictably, people were somewhat confused about why we were choosing to do this. Some people would text us, positive they had misunderstood the invitation. Surely it’s not everyone you know? Everyone? In one bar? Total and complete chaos? Yes, we’d say. It is indeed. You have not misunderstood. Please join us!

My friend Carlyn, ever the event planner, secured Linen Hall in the East Village as our event space. (Shoutout to the good folks there—they promised us control of the AUX and have a cute bartender with an Irish accent.) We had around 250 people between yeses and maybes (woohoo), a smattering of can’t go’s (have fun with that FOMO), and a swath of people who simply didn’t respond (maybe out of confusion? Either way, lame).

When my friend Taylor brought up the fact that it would be nice to know which host attendees knew, I concocted the idea of the wristband. Each host would have one, and you would wear the wristband corresponding to the host who got you there. We gamified this to force people to interact, too—if you interacted with a new host, you could collect theirs and compare to other strange partygoers/potential friends or lovers.

I spent the weeks leading up to the party worried nobody would attend and we’d be sitting alone, the 7 of us, in a giant event hall, solemnly listening to No Hands by Wacka Flocka Flame. When the date rolled around, we showed up, took a picture before guests began arriving, and waited.

Spoiler alert: the party was so wildly successful, we threw a sequel in February 2025. The bar was packed both times with people, talking and laughing and flirting and dancing—and absolutely ravenous for wristbands. In the February 2025 version, we bought cheapo medals off Amazon to give to people who collected all seven, which a boyfriend-who-shall-not-be-named of an attendee would reportedly wear in bed later that night.

The debriefs after these events are the stuff of legend. A friend of mine who hadn’t been on a date in three years (by choice—a picky queen) got swooned by another friend’s old camp acquaintance. My out-of-town friend from Philly (who came in just for the occasion) told me he saw a guy fail to wash his hands coming out of the bathroom, so the offender was nicknamed Pee Hands in my friend group forevermore. I then forced Philly friend to meet Emily’s coworker as I knew friendship was their destiny, and they spent the next hour in a beautiful nerd-out over Dungeons and Dragons.

Two short dudes in twinning baseball caps chatted up host Clare and I and insisted they knew host Dana from a Thai cooking class, and we had to kick them out after we found out that was fat lie and they refused to tell us which host they actually knew. My friend from high school brought a chihuahua into the party via tote bag, immediately grabbing the attention of everyone within eyeshot. A former two-date Hinger match of a host showed up fully wearing a backpack and over-the-ear Beats headphones, then promptly left after 30 minutes. A rich college acquaintance flexed his gold Amex so hard that a group of 16 struggling 20-somethings persuaded him into buying them a round. Chaos was plentiful, and chaos was beautiful.

This idea was borne as a joke, sure, but it works because people really do crave connection. We live in an online world where spaces to meet new people are increasingly disappearing. We’re all stressed with busy jobs and busy lives and busy minds, and it’s nice to have someone else do the heavy lifting of finding a bar and inviting the cool people they know to come hang out. My pod of pals chose to do it, and what ensued was more friends and two hilarious, silly nights full of laughter and chaos. We have a third on the books already. Yeah, it’s an ridiculous idea, but so much of life is already ridiculous. Why not lean into it? Find some co-hosts and invite everyone you know to a bar. I promise—it’ll be fun.

/blog/post/an-nyc-community-garden-that-.title: An NYC Community Garden That Grew from an Oil Spill: McCarren Demo Garden
/blog/post/an-nyc-community-garden-that-.description: A conversation with Marissa about connecting with neighbors, finding community, and getting your hands dirty in Brooklyn.
h1: An NYC Community Garden That Grew from an Oil Spill: McCarren Demo Garden
h2: So… who planted the first seed? How did this little green haven sprout up in the middle of the city?
What’s a typical day in the garden?
What's one of the most memorable events or moments you've experienced at the garden so far?
If the Garden were a vegetable…
I saw the collaboration with Paloma coffee on the lavender pastry, who’s on your dream collab wish list next?
Any garden crushes? Do you ever “garden hop” for inspiration?
How does the Demo Garden connect with the community?
p: A convo with Marissa about connecting with neighbors and getting your hands dirty in Greenpoint 🌱

Tucked inside McCarren Park, the Demo Garden is more than just a patch of green — it’s a community-powered plot for growing food, sharing knowledge, and making Brooklyn a little bit wilder. Born out of environmental justice history and run by North Brooklyn Mutual Aid, the garden is equal parts classroom, pantry, and party.

Greenpoint is home to one of the largest oil spills in US history. In the 70s, Sister Francis Kress — in a hazmat suit — dove in to gather evidence and testified before Congress. The eventual $20M settlement from ExxonMobil helped fund local projects, and in 2015, the McCarren Demonstration Garden was one of them. It found new life in 2022 when North Brooklyn Mutual Aid developed a programming strategy, and the garden officially sprouted into what it is today.
(Side note: we grow in raised beds with clean, non-contaminated soil)

On shift days, volunteers water, harvest, weigh, log, and deliver produce to local community fridges. Events, on the other hand, cover anything from breathwork to pickles to bats — usually an hour long, and always packed. Both are worth checking out (just be sure to follow along, because events fill up fast)!

There have been a couple of potlucks that have been really fun and silly because everyone has brought a variation on the same dish -- cucumber salads, gallettes, etc... And it's always really nice to sit and share a meal with everyone. But my favorite event every year is the pumpkin carving. Iain Burke is a super talented pumpkin carver (that's a thing!) and its always fun to learn a new technique and see how everyone's creations turn out.
Easy! Come to open hours. The full volunteer calendar is at mccarren.garden.
Ooof I'm gonna cheat and say that we're cucumbers since they're our bumper crop most years! (A bumper crop refers to an exceptionally large harvest of crops.)
Don’t water the leaves — get that hose down to the roots. Watering leaves can actually cause disease!
Every fall, we host Harvest Dinners with local restaurants who turn our produce into garden-themed dishes. Past partners include Fornino’s, Paulie Gee’s, Edy’s, and Leroy’s.
As a dinner party enjoyer, I wouldn’t be mad about a future collab with Nura…

Shout out to Lentol Garden for the composter they gave us this year! And we're garden crazy, we love them all in the neighborhood. We take a couple field trips a year together to peep what everyone else is doing. This year we went to Stone Barns which was super cute and fun. Can't wait to go back!
We grow all sorts of tomato varieties, but my favorite is the one called “Girl’s Girl Weird Thing.” Best name ever.

We’re here to grow food for community fridges and host a classroom for learning about gardening and climate action. But really, it’s also a way to meet neighbors and plug into North Brooklyn Mutual Aid. Whether or not you’re into plants, it’s about building community together.
